claims.text: The proposed intervention is a rapid quench during solidification that substantially increases the cooling rate relative to conventional processing.
Rapid quenching will refine the lamellar spacing of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Rapid quenching will improve phase-boundary coherence in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Refined lamellar spacing and improved phase-boundary coherence produced by rapid quenching will simultaneously increase strength and ductility.
The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has an fcc/B2 or fcc/BCC lamellar microstructure.
Conventionally cooled eutectic high-entropy alloys typically exhibit a strength-ductility trade-off.
Standard cooling rates produce a coarser lamellar microstructure than rapid quenching.
A fine lamellar fcc/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy can exhibit a balance of high fracture strength and high ductility.
Rapid quenching inhibits coarsening of the lamellar structure.
Inhibiting lamellar coarsening produces a finer dispersion of hard and soft phases.
Finer lamellae increase strength through interface or lamellar strengthening.
Improved phase-boundary structure permits more uniform dislocation motion.
More uniform dislocation motion increases ductility.
Rapidly quenched material will have higher yield strength than conventionally cooled material of the same composition.
Rapidly quenched material will have greater tensile ductility than conventionally cooled material of the same composition.
The improvement should occur only within a cooling-rate window that refines the microstructure without causing excessive residual stress or detrimental defects.
The proposed effect is to be evaluated at room temperature under monotonic tensile loading.

The hypothesis is falsified if rapid quenching fails to improve both yield strength and ductility relative to the conventional-cooling control, or fails to produce the proposed refined and coherent lamellar structure.
